messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Erik is a 28-year-old social media manager who deployed to Afghanistan six years ago as a combat medic. During a routine convoy, his vehicle hit an IED. He crawled through wreckage to reach a fellow soldier whose leg was nearly severed, the bone visible through torn fabric. A medevac helicopter landed minutes later, its rotor blades hammering the air as Erik helped load the wounded man. That night, under fire again, he made a split-second decision to take cover behind a low wall instead of helping another soldier drag a casualty—a choice he now replays with shame. The memories come in disjoined flashes: the smell of diesel, a sergeant’s radio static, the weight of a litter, but never the whole sequence. Sometimes he feels the full panic and nausea without any accompanying image, which leaves him disoriented and convinced the event is too extreme to have really happened.

Back home, Erik moved in with his girlfriend and took a job curating a brand’s social feed. The role requires constant scanning of images—news clips, user posts, advertisements—and he quickly discovered his triggers. A photo of a hiking accident showing an open wound sends his heart racing; the distant sound of a helicopter from a construction site makes him duck in his chair. Driving with colleagues to offsite meetings forces him to grip the door handle, expecting an explosion. In response, Erik has built an elaborate system of avoidance. He unfollows any account that posts violent imagery, deletes military-related content before it reaches his feed, and walks out of rooms where he sees a police officer’s uniform. He rehearses every phone call or in-person interaction in his head beforehand, testing possible topics to steer clear of anything that might lead to questions about his service. He also refuses invitations to run or hike, arguing that “putting my body under stress” would only bring back the physical memory of combat.

The avoidance keeps him safe in the moment, but it also keeps the memories fresh and unprocessed. Each time he sidesteps a trigger—a YouTube thumbnail of a wounded veteran, a coworker’s mention of a military discount—the fragmented images stay raw, and his conviction deepens that he is permanently damaged, an outsider who cannot live a normal life. He has come to believe that someone else would not have frozen behind that wall; a better soldier would have gone for the second man. These appraisals make him hypervigilant. At night he lies rigid, unable to fall asleep because he needs to stay alert to imagined sounds. When his girlfriend touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he jolts and swats her hand away. He monitors her face for signs of pity or frustration.

Over the past few months, the loops have tightened. A single trigger—the sight of a child’s skinned knee in a playground photo—floods him with emotion without a clear memory, which in turn convinces him he is irreparably broken. That belief then makes him even more watchful for potential triggers, scanning his environment for uniforms, wounds, or aircraft sounds. His rehearsed conversations have made him socially stiff; his girlfriend complains he “scripts everything.” He stopped joining her for drives because being a passenger sets off flashbacks, and he now works from home exclusively, missing team meetings. His PCL-5 score is 56. What finally brought him to therapy was not the fear itself, but his girlfriend’s tearful question last week: “Do you even feel like you’re still here?” Erik hopes that talking about the memories might shrink them, but he is terrified that naming the fragments will only prove they are too real—and that he really is the person he fears he has become.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory influences or leads to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat influences or leads to triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies influence or lead to triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies influence or lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Sometimes he feels the full panic and nausea without any accompanying image, which leaves him disoriented and convinced the event is too extreme to have really happened.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because the memory came back so vividly in those disembodied waves, he began to see threads of it everywhere: in the way a certain shade of desert tan appeared in an advertisement, in the crackle of a walkie-talkie on a TV show, in the specific hum of a passing truck.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He monitors her face for signs of pity or frustration.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living at that pitch of alertness, he found the world had become dense with reminders he couldn't stop reading — the curve of a jacket sleeve, the way a door slammed shut, the smell of antiseptic in a pharmacy.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He also refuses invitations to run or hike, arguing that “putting my body under stress” would only bring back the physical memory of combat.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each place he avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round he walked to avoid the subway station was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened, making the trigger feel ever more present.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He rehearses every phone call or in-person interaction in his head beforehand, testing possible topics to steer clear of anything that might lead to questions about his service.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, his body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set.
<<<END>>>
